findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 12 Joint Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Both councils finance capital through under-borrowing—running down reserves instead of borrowing—despite growing debt requirements.
findings.detail: Both maintain under-borrowed positions: Adur sits £4.535m below its Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) throughout; Worthing's under-borrowing widens from £7.552m to £20.445m by 2028/29. This strategy finances capital by depleting cash balances rather than taking on new debt, dependent on interest rate forecasts.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown is unsustainable long-term; if rates don't fall as forecast, councils will be forced to borrow expensively or cut programmes.
findings.figures: Worthing under-borrowing: £7.552m (2025/26) to £20.445m (2028/29); Adur under-borrowing: £4.535m (constant)
findings.quote: The Councils are both currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need ... is being funded by running down cash balances and reserves

findings.paper_title: 2026.01.15 JAGC Item 12 Joint Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Worthing's capital programme collapses from £39.7m to £2.2m over three years.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure for Worthing falls from £39.653m (2025/26 estimate) to £2.230m (2028/29 estimate). Non-HRA capital drops from £39.653m to £2.230m. This sharp decline signals either deferred projects or a material change in investment plans.
findings.matters: A sudden collapse in capital investment can indicate either budget stress or cancelled regeneration schemes; lenders need to understand why.
findings.figures: Worthing capital expenditure 2025/26: £39.653m; 2028/29: £2.230m
findings.quote: Worthing Borough Council Capital expenditure 2025/26 Estimate £39.653m ... 2028/29 Estimate £2.230m

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: Significant reliance on commercial property investment income (£4.66m) with concentration risk and requirement for void-management reserves
findings.detail: The document notes that 'the other significant area of income are the strategic property investment funds [...] generated income of £4.66m' and acknowledges this creates concentration and market risk. A Property Investment Risk Reserve is being built to £1.45m to manage void periods and maintenance. This indicates the council has made a strategic choice to generate income from property, creating exposure to market conditions.
findings.matters: Commercial property valuations and rental income are cyclical and subject to market downturns. A council dependent on £4.66m from property investment faces income volatility that is not within its control. The need for a large void-management reserve signals known risk.
findings.figures: £4.66m property investment income (no year specified); Property Investment Risk Reserve provision £1.45m for void management.
findings.quote: the other significant area of income are the strategic property investment funds [...] generated income of £4.66m in [...]

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: General Fund Working Balance is below target at 8.2% of budget and requires ongoing contributions to rebuild to 9.7%
findings.detail: The council's working balance is currently £1.1m, representing 8.2% of the budget, below the established target of 6%-10% (currently aimed at 9.7%). The document states 'The working balance is currently projected to be too low at year end' and proposes contributions of £250k for 2026/27 and £100k per year thereafter to rebuild. This diverts resources from service investment and indicates the council has been drawing on reserves.
findings.matters: A low working balance leaves a council vulnerable to in-year shocks. It also indicates past deficits were absorbed by reserve drawdowns. A lender needs to know whether the council is genuinely sustainable or living off reserves.
findings.figures: Current working balance £1.1m (8.2% of budget); target 9.7%; forecast to reach £1.3m (9.7%) by 2027/28.
findings.quote: The working balance is currently projected to be too low at year end.

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand is creating £300k annual cost pressure with no identified solution, establishing a new structural cost
findings.detail: Housing Needs budget has been increased by £300k specifically for 'Increase to Housing budget (demand on TA)' in 2026/27. The medium-term plan identifies this as an ongoing 'Cost pressures from Housing' of £300k in 2026/27, dropping to £200k in 2028/29 but not eliminated. This is housing demand-driven and outside the council's control, yet reduces financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Homelessness and temporary accommodation costs are rising across the country and are often demand-driven and difficult to control. A lender will want to know whether this pressure is temporary or structural; here it appears to be ongoing.
findings.figures: £300k growth in Housing Needs for temporary accommodation in 2026/27; forecast to remain at £200k-£300k in future years.
findings.quote: Increase to Housing budget (demand on TA) 300

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: Current-year income performance is falling short of budget, with proposed fee increases assumed only to mitigate existing shortfalls, not create new income
findings.detail: The document reveals that 'the current year forecasts project a number of performance shortfalls against budget' and crucially, 'additional income from increases has not been included within the budget for 2026/27, it is assumed it will mitigate shortfalls currently being experienced between budget and performance.' This means fee increases are a recovery plan, not a source of new money. If they fail to deliver the assumed mitigation, the council has no buffer.
findings.matters: Income volatility is a material risk for lenders. A council unable to forecast its own income reliably, and planning to use defensive fee increases merely to offset existing shortfalls, signals weak commercial discipline and cash flow risk.
findings.figures: Proposed average fee increase of 2% across services; assumed to offset current budget shortfalls, not generate additional surplus.
findings.quote: additional income from increases has not been included within the budget for 2026/27, it is assumed it will mitigate shortfalls currently being experienced between budget and performance.

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: Council relies on 2.99% council tax increase to balance the 2026/27 budget; any lower increase triggers additional savings requirements
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is only balanced if council tax is increased by exactly 2.99%. The document explicitly states that if a lower increase is approved, 'additional savings will [be needed] the reserves to balance the budget.' At 1% increase, the council would raise £77.9k less; at 2.0%, £156k less. With limited savings capacity identified, this creates a rigid funding dependency.
findings.matters: Political pressure or resident resistance could force a lower council tax increase, leaving the council without a funding solution. This represents a risk that the stated balanced budget is contingent on a political choice that may not hold.
findings.figures: 2.99% increase yields £8.048m council tax income; 1% increase would yield £7.894m (£154k shortfall); 2.0% would yield £7.972m (£76k shortfall).
findings.quote: Members are asked to consider which level of council tax increase that they [...] a 2.99% increase would [...] a balanced budget and [...] additional savings will [...] the reserves to balance the budget.

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: Business Rates Reset moved Adur from retaining growth to owing back £9m, a structural adverse shift in baseline funding
findings.detail: The 2026/27 business rates reset fundamentally changed Adur's position. Previously, the council retained growth above baseline. The reset introduces a 'payback' obligation, moving Adur to a position where it must return £9m accumulated growth. The document notes this was 'the era' of retained growth worth £6.2m through April 2026, but this is now reversed. This is a one-time structural blow to the council's financial position.
findings.matters: Business rates are a significant portion of council funding. A £9m payback in one financial year materially compresses cash flow and reduces discretionary capacity. This kind of funding change is outside council control and represents a key systemic risk.
findings.figures: £9m payback obligation introduced in 2026/27 reset; previous retained growth era was £6.2m.
findings.quote: The Business Rates Reset has moved Adur from a position of 'retained growth' to a position of 'payback' of £9m.

findings.paper_title: Adur Cabinet - Budget Estimates 2026_27 and setting of the 2026_27 Council Tax
findings.headline: Cumulative budget shortfalls grow from £0.5m in 2028/29 to £2.5m by 2030/31, requiring significant future savings
findings.detail: The council projects a balanced 2026/27 budget, but this deteriorates sharply in the medium term. By 2029/30, the cumulative shortfall reaches £1.7m, and by 2030/31 it reaches £2.5m. The document explicitly states 'Annual Savings to be found' of £134k in 2027/28 growing to £836k by 2030/31. This indicates the council faces material budget gaps that cannot be closed by current proposals.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can sustain its debt obligations and service quality. Growing, multi-year shortfalls suggest the council is consuming reserves or delaying difficult decisions, both risks to financial stability.
findings.quote: Current projected cumulative shortfall/(surplus) 0 134 510 1,709 2,545

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation announced with unknown timetable and no budgeted transition costs; merger of two to three HRAs including Adur
findings.detail: The paper states: 'Preparations will soon commence in relation to LGR once the new council/s foot print is known focusing on the merging of two or three HRAs including Adur Homes.' No specific provision has been made in the 2026/27 base budget for LGR delivery costs; the council assumes 'transitional funding required in 2026/27 will be financed via the Retained Business Rates Pool.' The precise timing and partnership implications remain 'contingent upon the final unitary model determined by Central Government.'
findings.matters: LGR uncertainty creates execution risk and contingent costs that are not yet quantified or funded. A merger of HRAs could affect debt allocation, operational efficiency, and financial reporting, with costs potentially exceeding available contingency.
findings.figures: No specific provision budgeted for LGR costs in 2026/27
findings.quote: Preparations will soon commence in relation to LGR once the new council/s foot print is known focusing on the merging of two or three HRAs including Adur Homes...no specific provision for LGR delivery costs has been included in the base budget. It is assumed that any transitional funding required in 2026/27 will be financed via the Retained Business Rates Pool.

findings.headline: Right to Buy stock losses continue; new government policies improve receipt retention but do not reverse underlying inventory decline
findings.detail: Council housing stock has declined from 2,617 units (2015/16) to estimated 2,615 (2026/27). RTB sales remain an ongoing loss (7-21 units per year in recent actuals). Though government policy from April 2026 now allows 100% retention of RTB receipts (previously there was 'Treasury Share' pooling) and extends the 5-year spending window to 10 years for future receipts, the underlying trajectory is still declining stock relative to demand.
findings.matters: RTB sales permanently shrink the income-generating asset base. Even with improved retention of capital receipts, the council cannot easily replace lost stock due to land constraints. This compounds income pressures and reduces the financial resilience of the HRA.
findings.figures: Stock 2015/16: 2,617 units; 2026/27 estimate: 2,615 units; RTB sales in 2024/25: 7 units (actual); 2026/27: estimated 8 units
findings.quote: The sustained loss of social housing stock through Right to Buy remains a critical risk to the HRA's viable asset base. While the government's review of RTB discounts (announced Autumn 2024) has impacted application rates, the replacement of sold units remains challenging due to land availability and development costs.

findings.headline: Capital programme severely constrained: £10.5m borrowing approved only covers backlog maintenance; no capacity for new build or estate regeneration
findings.detail: The council states explicitly: 'there is currently no capacity outside of improvement work to deliver new homes or regenerate our estates.' Stock condition surveys identified significant investment needs, and the council is borrowing £10.5m to address backlog maintenance and compliance work. This constrains the HRA's strategic options and limits growth in rental income through new stock.
findings.matters: Inability to grow stock or regenerate estates limits future revenue growth and means the council cannot easily escape its structural income deficit through portfolio expansion. This is a strategic constraint on long-term sustainability.
findings.figures: £10.5m new borrowing approved for capital programme 2026/27-2027/28
findings.quote: there is currently no capacity outside of improvement work to deliver new homes or regenerate our estates. This is a priority that we will be focused on as part of Local Government Reorganisation and Development.

findings.headline: Unsustainable long-term position: 30-year forecast shows HRA moving to recurring deficits despite 2026/27 surplus, driven by rising debt financing costs
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget shows a small £191k surplus, but the 30-year business plan explicitly states: 'HRA is not expected to remain in surplus in future years due to the increasing pressures of debt financing.' The plan forecasts net costs increasing substantially in later years as interest charges on rising debt accumulate. Interest on capital programme debt alone grows from £1.1m (2026/27) to £10.3m by 2054/55.
findings.matters: The council is borrowing £10.5m for 2026/27 capital and expecting a temporary surplus through rent increases, but underlying structural deficits are baked into the long-term forecast. This signals unsustainability without further rent increases or cost reductions.
findings.figures: 2026/27 surplus £191k; interest on new borrowing alone grows from £1,127k (2026/27) to £10,344k (2054/55) in 30-year plan
findings.quote: the HRA is not expected to remain in surplus in future years due to the increasing pressures of debt financing. Whilst it is predicted that the level of the general reserves will be at around 7% for 2026/27, the 30-year business plan expects that the reserves will gradually increase to more prudent levels over the next 5 years.

findings.headline: Permanent £2 million annual income loss from expired four-year government rent reduction (2016-2020) continues to constrain borrowing and investment capacity
findings.detail: The mandatory 1% rent reduction imposed by government from 2016-2020 permanently lowered the council's rental base by approximately £2 million per annum. Although the rent reduction regime has ended, 'the cumulative loss of income continues to impact long-term investment capacity.' This legacy shortfall directly constrains the council's ability to fund capital programmes and borrow for improvements.
findings.matters: A permanent £2m annual structural income deficit affects debt servicing capacity and limits the council's ability to invest in stock quality or support new build programmes, directly impacting long-term financial viability.
findings.figures: £2m per annum estimated historic loss of revenue
findings.quote: the cumulative loss of income continues to impact long-term investment capacity. The HRA has since transitioned to the current rent standard (effective from 2020/21).

findings.headline: Rent arrears escalating to nearly 1,000 tenants amid data systems failures and collection weaknesses
findings.detail: Almost 1,000 tenants are in rent arrears at varying levels, with 72 tenants owing £3,000 or more. The paper attributes this rise to legacy systems creating 'significant backlog of historic data in need of review and alignment' and identifies 'challenges in relation to accurate data' and 'ability to work with tenants...to effectively collect income.' Universal Credit migration exacerbates this with a five-week waiting period for new claims creating 'technical arrears.'
findings.matters: Arrears growth indicates income collection risk and suggests underlying operational/IT failures affecting receivables control. With two-thirds of tenants on Housing Benefit or UC, welfare reform creates structural collection risk that lenders need to price into any refinancing decisions.
findings.figures: £3000+: 72 tenants; £1000-£3000: 191 tenants; £500-£1000: 185 tenants; £1-£500: 707 tenants; approximately 1,000 tenants total in arrears
findings.quote: overall arrears have been increasing with almost 1000 tenants in rent arrears to differing levels...our legacy systems have created a number of challenges in relation to accurate data and though work is underway to address these issues, there is a significant backlog of historic data in need of review and alignment.

findings.headline: Regulator self-referral for housing compliance issues still unresolved after nearly three years
findings.detail: The council self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing in May 2023. As of this January 2026 report, improvements are ongoing and the council has not yet exited the enhanced regulatory oversight. Success of audit outcomes will inform a decision to conclude the self-referral. A full inspection by the regulator is anticipated once compliance standards are met.
findings.matters: Unresolved regulatory breaches indicate operational risk, compliance failures, and capital asset management problems that could affect the council's ability to service debt or maintain stock quality.
findings.figures: Self-referral May 2023; report dated January 2026
findings.quote: We are now almost three years into the improvement plan and meet monthly with the Regulator of Social Housing to review progress and actions required for continuous development.

findings.headline: £3.5m organisational redesign savings now embedded in base budget; final workstreams carry over into 2026/27
findings.detail: Over two years, the councils ran a major organisational redesign generating £3.5m in savings that are now part of the base budget. However, final workstreams are "expected to carry over into 2026/27", meaning the transformation is not yet complete. Earlier in the same year the councils announced Housing Needs savings slippages, showing delivery is at risk.
findings.matters: Unfinished transformation programmes carry execution risk. If final workstreams slip further or do not materialise, embedded savings of this scale could be at risk, widening the budget shortfalls already visible in the MTFP.
findings.figures: £3.5m of savings embedded in core budget from redesign programme
findings.quote: Over the previous two years the councils have been working through the implementation of a significant organisational redesign programme with over £3.5m of savings embedded in the core budget. Final workstreams of delivery are expected to carry over into 2026/27.

findings.headline: Partnership at risk: financial positions of Adur and Worthing councils diverging, creating structural strain
findings.detail: The paper explicitly warns that the two councils' financial positions are not the same, and describes asymmetry in financial capacity as "a considerable risk for both councils and the share service arrangement." The councils are taking unequal shares of growth (Worthing £3.5m vs Adur £1.1m in 2026/27), reflecting different underlying pressures.
findings.matters: Shared services arrangements depend on both partners remaining broadly financially viable. If one council weakens materially, the partnership becomes a liability for both. This paper shows strain is already visible.
findings.figures: Worthing share of joint budget 2026/27 £18.24m, Adur £13.25m. Worthing growth allocation £3.534m, Adur £1.084m
findings.quote: However, the financial positions of the two councils are not the same. This brings with it risk for the partnership as any asymmetry in the capacity of each council needs to be addressed in the shared delivery model. It remains a considerable risk for both councils and the share service arrangement.

findings.headline: Central government funding settlement at risk; final decision due February 2026 with potential for reduction
findings.detail: The councils received a provisional settlement in December 2025 but are waiting for the final settlement in early February 2026. The paper explicitly flags "a potential risk of a reduction in local funding allocations" and states this "will initially be managed through reserve provisions, but a significant reduction may necessitate decisions affecting the joint service budget." If the reduction is material, they may need to revise the budget downward after setting council tax.
findings.matters: Pending funding decisions expose the councils to potential mid-year budget revisions. A material reduction could force service cuts or larger reserve depletion than planned.
findings.figures: 2026/27 joint budget requirement £31,488,710; settlement decision due 3 weeks after this budget was set
findings.quote: the final settlement is expected in early February 2026 with a potential risk of a reduction in local funding allocations. This risk will initially be managed through reserve provisions, but a significant reduction may necessitate decisions affecting the joint service budget.

findings.headline: Budget shortfalls forecast to grow from £19k in 2027/28 to £2.3m by 2031, with no identified savings solutions
findings.detail: The councils' five-year forecast shows cumulative shortfalls building across the period: £19k in 2027/28, £872k in 2028/29, £1.49m in 2029/30, and £2.29m by 2030/31. The paper acknowledges shortfalls "will continue to have budget shortfalls for at least the next 2 - 5 years" and states there will need to be savings, but provides no specific proposals or delivery plans for how they will be found.
findings.matters: Cumulative, unresolved budget shortfalls over multiple years signal structural fiscal stress. Without identified solutions, these gaps will require either service reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.quote: following settlement, it is clear that the Councils will continue to have budget shortfalls for at least the next 2 - 5 years

findings.headline: Housing Needs savings plan failed to deliver; demand growth forces £2.1m additional budget allocation in 2026/27
findings.detail: The councils had planned savings in Housing Needs that did not materialise in 2025/26. Demand for temporary accommodation rose instead, forcing them to build growth into the 2026/27 budget: £300k for Adur and £1.8m for Worthing. The paper explicitly states the savings slipped and cost pressures forced growth instead.
findings.matters: A service where planned savings didn't deliver and cost pressures are rising is a first-order concern for lenders. Housing and temporary accommodation costs are a known flashpoint in councils and this shows it is happening here.
findings.figures: Housing Needs growth 2026/27: Adur £300,000, Worthing £1,800,000, total £2,100,000
findings.quote: Within the Housing Needs service there has been some delay in saving delivery in the current year and this has been compounded by increasing demand pressure, to address the ongoing cost pressures growth has been built into the 2026/27 budget for both Adur and Worthing

findings.headline: Housing Needs service was seriously overspent in 2025/26 and faces ongoing budget impacts
findings.detail: The Housing Needs Manager reported that the service significantly exceeded its 2025/26 budget and expects serious budget pressures to continue into future years.
findings.matters: An ongoing service overspend indicates either uncontrolled demand pressures or cost inflation the council cannot absorb. Persistent overspends force either service cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: amount of overspend not stated
findings.quote: the Housing Needs Manager reported on the current budget situation for the Housing Needs service and the reasons why the budget was seriously overspent for 2025/26 and likely to be seriously impacted on in future years.

findings.headline: Joint partner Worthing has requested £5 million emergency funding from Government to balance its 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: Worthing's transformation plans cannot close its significant budget gap. The council has formally requested £5 million exceptional funding support from MHCLG, including borrowing costs. Worthing's balanced budget is also contingent on maximum 3% Council Tax increase.
findings.matters: A lender to Adur should understand that its joint partner is in financial distress requiring government bailout to balance. This creates governance risk, potential for service disruption, and reputational/operational interdependence if services are shared.
findings.figures: £5 million
findings.quote: Worthing was predicted to set a balanced budget but to achieve that the Council had requested up to £5 million emergency funding support from the Government which included borrowing costs

findings.headline: Council is using capital flexibilities to fund transformation costs rather than capital investment
findings.detail: The Working Group noted a proposal to use capital flexibilities (temporary permission to use capital receipts for revenue) to fund additional resources for Local Government Reorganisation transformation workstreams.
findings.matters: Capital flexibilities are exceptional temporary tools. Using them for transformation rather than asset investment indicates the council cannot afford change costs from revenue, suggesting deeper budget pressure.
findings.figures: not quantified in paper
findings.quote: there was a proposal to use capital flexibilities to fund additional resource to support transformation workstreams for both councils.

findings.headline: Government grant funding for 2026/27 specifically excludes costs for food waste collections
findings.detail: Despite a slightly larger grant allocation than previous years, the additional funding is minimal and does not cover food waste collection costs, creating an unfunded statutory service commitment.
findings.matters: Food waste collections are a statutory duty. Councils must fund this from existing revenue or cut other services; it represents an unfunded commitment that reduces financial flexibility and could require reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: no allocation provided
findings.quote: the additional funding was minimal and would not include allocations for the costs of food waste collections.

findings.headline: Adur's balanced budget for 2026/27 depends entirely on achieving the maximum 3% Council Tax increase
findings.detail: The council has no flexibility to balance its budget if it needs to increase Council Tax by less than the maximum permitted 3%. This indicates tight budget headroom with no contingency for shortfalls in Council Tax collection or policy changes restricting increases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can manage if its main revenue lever is constrained. Zero flexibility on tax raises the likelihood of future reliance on reserves or borrowing.
findings.quote: Adur was set to report a balanced budget position but on the assumption that there would be the maximum increase in council tax of 3%.

findings.paper_title: Joint Mid Year Treasury Management Review 2025/26
findings.headline: Investment portfolio yields declining year-on-year
findings.detail: Adur's investment yield has fallen from 4.67% p.a. in 2024/25 to 4.21% p.a. in the first half of 2025/26. The decline reflects the councils' deliberate strategy to prioritize internal borrowing and preserve liquidity for capital funding rather than committing funds to longer-term deposits.
findings.matters: Declining investment returns reduce the councils' non-service revenue streams and signal tightening cash positions; this constrains financial flexibility and may require deeper service cuts or reserves drawdown if budgets come under pressure.
findings.figures: Adur: 4.21% p.a. vs prior year 4.67% p.a.; Worthing portfolio yield 4.596% p.a.
findings.quote: The term deposit and liquidity portfolio yield for the first six months of the year is 4.21% p.a. (2025 4.67% p.a.). The other investment held by the council is a £3m investment in the Local Authorities' Property Fund, for which we project a return of 3.88% p.a.

findings.paper_title: Joint Mid Year Treasury Management Review 2025/26
findings.headline: Close Brothers Ltd removed from approved counterparty list following credit rating downgrade
findings.detail: Both councils have suspended and formally removed Close Brothers from their approved investment counterparty list following an FCA investigation into historical motor finance commissions. The bank's Fitch rating has fallen to BBB with negative outlook, below the councils' minimum A- requirement. Recovery is not expected in the near term, with FCA complaint handling paused until May 2026.
findings.matters: A counterparty falling below investment grade signals active credit deterioration and demonstrates the councils' credit monitoring discipline, but also highlights vulnerability in their banking relationships and potential liquidity constraints if other counterparties face similar stress.
findings.figures: Close Brothers: Fitch rating BBB with Negative Outlook; FCA complaint pause until May 2026; final redress rules not expected until mid-2026
findings.quote: Both councils have previously suspended dealing with Close Brothers Ltd; action has been taken to remove the bank from the approved counterparty list of both Councils. This action follows the sustained pressure on the bank's credit profile resulting from the Financial Conduct Authority's (FCA) investigation into historical motor finance commissions.

findings.paper_title: Joint Mid Year Treasury Management Review 2025/26
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement more than doubled as capital spend increases
findings.detail: Adur's borrowing need jumped from £9.536m to £28.268m; Worthing's from £10.150m to £24.977m. The increase reflects the elevated capital expenditure forecasts and represents a material expansion of the councils' debt-financed investment.
findings.matters: A near-tripling of borrowing needs signals increased debt servicing costs and refinancing exposure, affecting the councils' debt capacity and the debt sustainability ratios lenders monitor.
findings.figures: Adur borrowing requirement: £28.268m revised vs £9.536m original; Worthing: £24.977m revised vs £10.150m original
findings.quote: The borrowing element of the tables increases the underlying indebtedness of the Councils by way of the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), although this will be reduced in part by revenue charges for the repayment of debt (the Minimum Revenue Provision).

findings.paper_title: Joint Mid Year Treasury Management Review 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure estimates nearly doubled, driven by unspent prior-year budgets
findings.detail: Adur's capital expenditure revised upward from £14.452m to £33.794m, with £16.9m attributable to budgets carried forward from 2024/25 that were not spent. Worthing similarly revised from £18.761m to £39.653m with £17.4m in carry-forwards. This represents significant timing slippage in the councils' capital delivery.
findings.matters: Large carry-forwards signal delays in capital execution, which directly inflate borrowing requirements and affect debt serviceability metrics that lenders use to assess financial risk and planning accuracy.
findings.figures: Adur revised estimate £33.794m (original £14.452m); Worthing revised estimate £39.653m (original £18.761m)
findings.quote: The change in the Adur capital expenditure estimate is due mainly to the budgets brought forward from last year, which were not spent, this was approved in the capital outturn report and accounts for a £16.9m of increase.

findings.paper_title: Joint Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Forecasted investment income return only 3.63-3.50% while borrowing costs are significantly higher
findings.detail: The councils' budgeted investment earnings rates are 3.63% for 2026/27 and 3.50% for 2027/28 onwards. Meanwhile, PWLB borrowing rates are substantially higher. This creates a negative carry: borrowing costs exceed investment returns, meaning the gap between the cost of debt service and income from reserves is widening.
findings.matters: A widening gap between borrowing costs and investment returns reduces the councils' financial flexibility and means reserves are eroding in real terms. This is unsustainable if debt continues to grow while investment returns decline.
findings.figures: Investment return 2026/27: 3.63%. 2027/28: 3.50%. 2028/29: 3.50%. MUFG long-term PWLB forecast: 3.50% (but short-term rates higher)

findings.paper_title: Joint Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Worthing has £10m loan to Worthing Homes and £3.684m outstanding to GB Met College - service investments at credit risk
findings.detail: Worthing is providing non-treasury loans to third parties: a £10m 10-year loan to its housing company Worthing Homes, and a £5m 20-year loan to GB Met College of which £3.684m remains outstanding. These are listed as service investments, not treasury investments, and are secured on the borrower's assets, creating credit exposure.
findings.matters: If either borrower runs into difficulty, Worthing would face losses and loss of repayment. These loans constrain the council's available liquidity and represent contingent liabilities if either borrower's financial position deteriorates.
findings.figures: Worthing Homes loan: £10m (10 years). GB Met College: £5m facility with £3.684m remaining to be repaid over 20 years.
findings.quote: a £10m loan to Worthing Homes ●  a £5m repayment loan to GBMet College, with £3.684m remaining

findings.paper_title: Joint Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Substantial commercial property debt exposure: Adur 42% of debt, Worthing 32% of debt
findings.detail: Adur has £74.872m in debt relating to commercial property (42% of total external debt as of March 2025), declining to 32% by 2028/29. Worthing has £67.209m in commercial property debt (32% of total as of March 2025). This exposure to commercial real estate is significant given current market volatility in office and retail property.
findings.matters: Commercial property valuations are volatile. If property values decline, councils face potential impairment charges and refinancing risk. This concentration of debt against a specific asset class limits flexibility and creates market-dependent risk.
findings.figures: Adur commercial debt: £74.872m (42% of total). Worthing commercial debt: £67.209m (32% of total).
findings.quote: Within the above figures the level of debt relating to commercial property is:  Actual debt at 31 March £m  (74.872)

findings.paper_title: Joint Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 23-24% over four years
findings.detail: Adur's total CFR is forecast to grow from £184.834m (2024/25 actual) to £228.912m (2028/29 estimate), an increase of £44.078m. Worthing's CFR grows from £215.94m to £266.29m, an increase of £50.35m. This represents significant structural growth in borrowing need driven by capital programmes.
findings.matters: A rising CFR indicates growing indebtedness and higher annual debt service costs. These forecasts suggest both councils will be borrowing more each year, which compounds interest burden and limits financial flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Joint Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: EFS borrowing creates long-term obligations without creating physical assets
findings.detail: The councils are using Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) borrowing to stabilise budgets. Unlike normal capital borrowing which funds infrastructure, EFS borrowing does not create any physical asset, meaning the debt burden grows without the corresponding asset base. This represents borrowing purely to cover revenue shortfalls.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether debt is backed by asset creation (capital borrowing) or is simply covering revenue gaps. EFS debt is essentially unsecured against future income and represents structural budget weakness.
findings.quote: Members should note that EFS borrowing does not create a physical asset, unlike other capital borrowing conducted

findings.paper_title: 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: PWLB lending restrictions since 2021 prevent the council from funding new property investments for yield, blocking growth strategy
findings.detail: Revised PWLB criteria introduced in 2021 increased scrutiny on borrowing and explicitly prevent local authorities from using PWLB loans to fund new investments primarily for yield. This regulatory constraint, combined with geographic restrictions (must invest only within the council's area), explains the three-year freeze on acquisitions and the lack of opportunities for future growth.
findings.matters: The council cannot borrow its way out of the deficit through property investment, because the government has closed the funding mechanism that previously enabled this strategy. This materially limits its options for revenue generation.
findings.figures: PWLB rates have ranged from below 1% to in excess of 6% during the last decade (3.3). Average lot size adjusted to £2m-£25m due to 'locational restrictions on lending' (14.13).
findings.quote: Revised 2021 onward PWLB Funding arrangements resulted in increased scrutiny on borrowing, preventing the use of this loan facility to fund new investments primarily for yield.

findings.paper_title: 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Property investment acquisitions have ceased for three years and portfolio is likely to shrink unless new purchases resume
findings.detail: No new purchases have been made for over three years (last purchase November 2022). Officers expect no substantial new opportunities in 2026. The portfolio will 'maintain the same component properties or shrink over the budget period of two years unless new acquisitions are made'. A selective disposal programme has begun. The fund is contracting, not growing.
findings.matters: A shrinking asset base means declining income in the medium term, compounding the council's budget challenge, particularly as it depends on this income to manage its deficit.
findings.figures: No acquisitions since November 2022. Fund size approved at £125m per council but available budget has been reduced after capital programme reviews (18.3).
findings.quote: During the last financial year, no new purchases were made, the last being in November 2022.

findings.paper_title: 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: MEES energy efficiency compliance will require substantial capital investment by a legally binding 2030 deadline
findings.detail: A minimum Energy Performance Certificate threshold of A/B/C becomes legally binding in 2030 for all lettable space. Officers have already identified shortfalls across the portfolio and are planning to address them through a revised capital programme. The council notes that properties will become unlettable at lower grades, directly threatening income.
findings.matters: This creates a defined capital spending obligation that could compete with debt servicing and other budget priorities, especially given the council's deficit position. Failure to comply means loss of lettable space and income.
findings.figures: 2030 is the compliance deadline. Current provision for maintenance/voids is £850k for Adur and £750k for Worthing annually (18.6).
findings.quote: There will be a minimum Energy Performance Certificate threshold of A/B/C in 2030 beyond which it will be illegal to let space at a lower grade. Officers have identified shortfalls and are planning to address this through a revised capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Tenant defaults are occurring and creating bad debts as the investment environment deteriorates
findings.detail: Two smaller tenants and a household-name tenant have failed. Two additional late rent payments became bad debts through tenant liquidation. Retail and hospitality tenants remain under active concern and being monitored. The overall rent collection rate is 97%, meaning 3% of income is at risk.
findings.matters: If the council's primary income stream from property investment is failing, this directly undermines both the revenue budget it depends on and the council's ability to service debt used to acquire these properties.
findings.figures: Rent collection approximately 97% of all rents across occupied properties. Two of the late payments turned into bad debts through tenant liquidation. Overall portfolio collecting 97% means 3% impairment.
findings.quote: However two of the smaller tenants have failed, as has a household name, and others especially in retail and hospitality, remain a concern and are being monitored.

findings.paper_title: 9 Strategic Property Investment Fund - Annual Commercial Property Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council's deficit position is directly affecting property investment strategy and forcing focus on survival over growth
findings.detail: In 2025, officers refocused efforts away from acquisitions to preserve revenue through rent collection and tenant engagement, because the council's deficit position made the investment strategy unsustainable. Property income is a core element of the 2026/27 budget and future budgets: the councils depend on this fund to manage continued financial pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the income the council is relying on to service existing debt and fund operations is being squeezed by the council's own deficit, not by market opportunity.
findings.figures: SPIF property rental income makes up 64% of Adur's non-residential property income (section 6.7). The contribution from SPIF investments is a 'core element of future budgets' (16.3).
findings.quote: The investment strategy is significantly affected by the Council's deficit position so in 2025 officers re-focused their efforts on rent collection and tenant engagement, to preserve the Council's revenue position.

findings.headline: Auditors investigating objections to 2024/25 accounts regarding Strategic Property Investment Fund (SPIF) financial performance, valuation, management, and cost overruns at Worthing Integrated Care Centre (WICC)
findings.detail: Members of the public have objected to the Adur District Council accounts (Worthing's joint body) raising concerns about SPIF financial performance, value, management, and issues and cost overruns including at WICC. These objections are not eligible under Adur rules but EY is considering them as information provided to the auditor. The audit work on these matters is ongoing.
findings.matters: Major capital projects in financial trouble (cost overruns, underperformance) indicate poor project governance and represent potential future bailouts or asset write-downs. This directly affects the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: Public objections received on SPIF and WICC; audit work ongoing
findings.quote: We received two objections to the 2024/25 accounts of Adur District Council from members of the public... due to the joint arrangement between the Councils we are considering the matters raised as information provided to the auditor for the 2024/25 audit.

findings.headline: Quality of financial data and supporting evidence below audit standard in multiple areas; contract register, lease schedule, and fixed asset register all materially inaccurate
findings.detail: Audit identified systemic data quality problems: contract register has incorrect values and missing documentation; lease schedule shows incorrect rent, break clauses, and expiry dates; fixed asset register included assets sold years earlier (Teville Gate and Durrington Station car parks). Supporting evidence across creditors, debtors, income and expenditure lacked sufficient detail and reliability.
findings.matters: Poor data quality suggests the council's financial systems are not producing reliable information. This increases the risk of errors cascading through the accounts and suggests weak financial control discipline.
findings.figures: Multiple reconciliation failures across contract register, lease schedule, and fixed asset register; two car parks remained on FAR after sale
findings.quote: Our review of the Council's contract register identified several inconsistencies between the register and the underlying contract documentation... These discrepancies indicate weaknesses in the accuracy and completeness of the contract register data

findings.headline: Investment properties overstated by £2.537 million; multiple other valuation misstatements totalling over £3.6 million identified
findings.detail: EY's own valuation experts found four investment properties outside expected ranges by £2.537 million (overstated). Additionally, PPE valuation errors of £0.555 million (Museum/Art Gallery, wrong obsolescence percentage), £0.430 million (indexation error), and Grafton multi-storey car park impairment of £0.097 million (closed due to structural issues). These are uncorrected misstatements that management is expected to adjust.
findings.matters: Large asset valuation misstatements indicate the council's valuers are not reliable and the council's asset base may be materially overstated. This affects the council's borrowing capacity and the true value of its property portfolio.
findings.figures: Investment properties overstated £2.537 million; PPE DRC error £0.555 million; PPE indexation error £0.430 million; Grafton car park impairment £0.097 million; total identified audit differences exceed £3.6 million
findings.quote: Our investment properties valuation testing identified a total difference of £2.537 million in judgment between the EY valuation specialist and the Council's specialist valuer, which suggests that the valuation of the asset is overstated.

findings.headline: Auditors cannot yet issue full audit opinion; will likely issue qualified opinion rather than disclaimer but assurance gaps on PPE and reserves will persist
findings.detail: Despite auditing the closing balance sheet and in-year transactions, EY has not obtained sufficient evidence for full reasonable assurance. The disclaimer on 2023/24 means brought-forward balances lack assurance. By the 27 February 2026 backstop date, EY will not be able to rebuild assurance on Property, Plant & Equipment and Reserves balances. A qualified opinion (not a full clean opinion) is now more likely than another disclaimer.
findings.matters: A qualified opinion means the audited accounts carry uncertainty over significant asset values and reserve positions. This creates doubt about the reliability of the council's balance sheet and its true financial position.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026; assurance gaps on PPE and Reserves balances; 2024/25 still under reset/recovery arrangements
findings.quote: In 2024/25, we have continued to audit the closing balance sheet and in-year transactions. Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances.

findings.headline: Internal audit issued Limited Assurance Opinion for second consecutive year, with seven Limited and three Unsatisfactory Assurance reviews identifying systemic control weaknesses
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's draft 2024/25 opinion is again Limited Assurance (same as 2023/24), reflecting persistent and systemic control deficiencies. Out of 22 audit reviews, seven received Limited Assurance and three Unsatisfactory Assurance ratings. Root causes include lack of robust monitoring, inadequate documentation, resource constraints, immature project management, and poor data quality across systems.
findings.matters: Two consecutive limited assurance opinions indicate the council's internal control framework is fundamentally weak. This increases the risk of material errors, fraud, and operational failure going undetected.
findings.figures: 22 internal audit reviews; 7 Limited Assurance; 3 Unsatisfactory Assurance; 4 Moderate Assurance
findings.quote: The HoIA issued a Limited Assurance Opinion for 2023/24. However, based on the draft 2024/25 Internal Annual Report, the HoIA's Opinion for the current financial year is also anticipated to be Limited Assurance. This continuity of a limited assurance opinion across two consecutive financial years underscores a persistent and systemic issue with the effectiveness of the Council's internal control framework.

findings.headline: Risk of Section 114 Notice (statutory insolvency warning) significantly increased by continued financial deterioration
findings.detail: The auditors flag that the continued deterioration in the council's financial position significantly increases the risk that the Section 151 Officer may need to issue a Section 114 Notice under the Local Government Finance Act 1988. This notice is required when expenditure is likely to exceed available resources. The s151 officer is considering whether to issue one whilst seeking extended EFS from MHCLG.
findings.matters: A Section 114 Notice is a formal declaration of financial distress that triggers government intervention, restrictions on spending, and often audit investigation. It signals institutional failure and is the severest form of financial warning a council can issue.
findings.figures: Section 114 Notice risk assessment performed; discussions with MHCLG ongoing on extending EFS
findings.quote: In our view, the continued deterioration in the Council's financial position significantly increases the risk that a Section 114 Notice may need to be issued. The s151 officer may need to seek legal advice on their decision whether to issue a Section 114 Notice whilst discussions regarding extending the exceptional financial support with MHCLG are ongoing.

findings.headline: Reserves projected to fall to £0.111 million, critically below the council's own 6-10% policy range and well below minimum prudent levels
findings.detail: After funding the reported overspend, available reserves are projected to fall from £1.580 million to £0.111 million. This is described as critically low and severely limits the council's ability to absorb future financial shocks. For a council with £15+ million annual revenue spend, reserves of £0.111 million represent only 0.7% of spending, creating acute vulnerability.
findings.matters: Reserves below minimum safe levels indicate the council has no buffer for unexpected pressures. This is a key indicator that the council is financially distressed and cannot manage normal operational variance.
findings.figures: Projected reserves fall from £1.580 million to £0.111 million; policy range is 6-10% of net revenue expenditure; General Fund budget £15.225 million
findings.quote: The Council's reserves remain critically low. After funding the reported overspend, available reserves are projected to fall from £1.580 million to £0.111 million—well below the recommended policy range of 6–10% of net revenue expenditure.

findings.headline: Council unable to set balanced budget for 2025/26 without £2 million exceptional financial support, with overspends now deteriorating month-on-month
findings.detail: The council has faced sustained financial pressures from housing demand and supported accommodation growth since 2022/23. After requesting £2 million in Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from MHCLG, the council is now likely to request additional funding for 2025/26 and extend support into 2026/27. Q2 2025/26 monitoring shows a net General Fund overspend of £4.115 million, up sharply from £1.469 million in Q1, indicating deteriorating control of spending.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot fund its operations from its own resources and is in structural deficit. Month-on-month deterioration suggests the council's spending controls are failing even with EFS in place.
findings.figures: £2 million EFS requested; Q1 2025/26 overspend £1.469 million; Q2 2025/26 overspend £4.115 million; 2024/25 outturn overspend £0.235 million; operational services overspend £0.855 million
findings.quote: the Council is unable to set a balanced budget for 2025/26 without additional funding. As a result, it has applied to the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government (MHCLG) for £2 million in EFS

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease standard not implemented in published 2024/25 accounts; council's initial lease assessment used incorrect definition.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts was published under IAS 17 rather than IFRS 16, which became mandatory from 1 April 2024. The council's initial assessment of which leases fell within scope excluded leases ending within the current year; IFRS 16 defines short-term leases by commencement date (12 months or less), not end date. The council has now re-examined its contract listing with the correct definition.
findings.matters: Failure to implement a mandatory accounting standard in published accounts is a compliance failure; the incorrect lease definition applied first indicates process gaps in the council's accounting policy review and implementation.
findings.figures: Published 2024/25 accounts continued to use IAS 17 framework rather than IFRS 16
findings.quote: The published 2024/25 Statement of Accounts continued to be prepared under IAS 17 rather than applying the requirements of IFRS 16. From our review of the Council's assessment, we noted that leases ending within the current financial year were excluded from consideration.

findings.headline: Quality of working papers and supporting evidence below acceptable standard across multiple areas including creditors, debtors, income, and expenditure.
findings.detail: The auditors reported that the quality of supporting evidence was 'generally below an acceptable standard in a number of areas.' Debtors and creditors working papers were presented in formats that made sampling difficult. Key areas lacked sufficient detail and reliability for audit verification. The council also struggled to provide timely, complete breakdowns of debtor and creditor balances at year-end, causing considerable delays and inefficiencies in the audit.
findings.matters: Poor documentation and evidence quality impairs the council's ability to demonstrate the accuracy of its financial statements, increases audit costs and timescales, and indicates gaps in finance function process discipline and quality assurance.
findings.figures: Rating: 'Requires improvement' for quality of working papers and supporting evidence; 'Requires improvement' for timeliness of draft financial statements delivery
findings.quote: The quality of the working papers provided was generally below an acceptable standard in a number of areas. Despite improvement from the prior year, working papers relating to debtors and creditors were presented in a format that made it difficult to select samples for testing.

findings.headline: Public Interest Report objections pending on Strategic Property Investment Fund, citing financial performance, value, management, and cost overruns including Albion Street Development.
findings.detail: Two members of the public have objected to the 2024/25 accounts, requesting the auditor issue a Public Interest Report regarding the Strategic Property Investment Fund (SPIF). The objections cite concerns about the fund's financial performance, its stated value, its management, and issues and cost overruns including the Albion Street Development project. The auditors' consideration of these matters is ongoing.
findings.matters: A capital project attracting public objections and a potential Public Interest Report signals reputational and possibly financial risk; cost overruns on major property development are often indicators of governance or commercial judgment issues that can affect council finances.
findings.figures: Two public objections received; work on assessment is in progress
findings.quote: We received two objections to the 2024/25 accounts from members of the public, requesting us to issue a Public Interest Report. Our consideration of the matters raised is in progress.

findings.headline: Adur Homes cut-off errors in invoice processing persist despite three testing extensions, creating recurring financial misstatements.
findings.detail: Auditors identified cut-off errors where invoices from 2023/24 were incorrectly recorded in 2024/25, arising from delays by Adur Homes in submitting invoices to the finance team. Testing was extended three times; each extension revealed similar errors. Post-year-end testing found invoices from 2024/25 recorded in 2025/26. Projected net misstatements: £0.213 million for council dwelling additions, £0.506 million for HRA expenditure. The auditors noted this indicates a control weakness within Adur Homes relating to timely submission and recording.
findings.matters: Recurring cut-off errors across three extended testing phases indicate a systemic failure in the Adur Homes finance processes and interface with the council's central finance team, creating risk of undetected misstatement in future periods and suggesting the control will not self-correct.
findings.figures: £0.213 million projected misstatement in PPE additions; £0.506 million in HRA expenditure; errors found across 2023/24, 2024/25, and 2025/26 periods
findings.quote: We extended our testing three times, and each extension continued to reveal similar errors. Considering these findings, we concluded that the issue was likely to affect post-year-end transactions as well, creating a risk of understatement of additions and HRA expenditure for the year.

findings.headline: Internal audit issued Limited Assurance opinion for second consecutive year, indicating systemic control framework weaknesses.
findings.detail: The head of internal audit's draft 2024/25 opinion is anticipated to be Limited Assurance again, following 2023/24. The report identified seven Limited Assurance and three Unsatisfactory Assurance reviews out of 22 total. Recurring root causes include insufficient oversight of contracts and property data, lack of documented policies, staff shortages and high turnover, immature project management, and poor data quality in systems—particularly in housing debt management and health & safety compliance reporting.
findings.matters: Second consecutive Limited Assurance opinion indicates the council's control environment is not effectively operating across multiple areas; the systemic nature (poor data quality, inadequate documentation, resource constraints) suggests improvements require corporate-level action, not isolated service fixes.
findings.figures: 7 Limited Assurance + 3 Unsatisfactory Assurance reviews out of 22 undertaken; 4 received Moderate Assurance
findings.quote: This continuity of a limited assurance opinion across two consecutive financial years underscores a persistent and systemic issue with the effectiveness of the Council's internal control framework.

findings.headline: Investment property valuations overstated by £3.955 million; multiple property accounting errors identified across PPE.
findings.detail: External valuation specialists found four investment properties outside the expected range by £3.954 million; separately, PPE indexation errors caused the Commerce Way Depot to be understated by £3.331 million. A misapplied Excel formula and incorrect index application affected multiple properties. An Ashcroft Development asset was incorrectly recorded, applying an impairment to the revaluation reserve instead of as a loss.
findings.matters: Material errors in property asset valuations (the council's largest balance sheet items) indicate weak controls over revaluation processes and specialist information management, creating risk of undetected misstatement.
findings.figures: Investment properties £3.955m overstatement; Commerce Way Depot £3.331m understatement; Old Customs House £0.073m understatement; HRA garages £0.445m overstatement; Ashcroft Development £1.829m impairment incorrectly recorded
findings.quote: Our investment properties valuation testing identified a total difference of £3.955 million in judgment between the EY valuation specialist and the Council's specialist valuer, which suggests that the valuation of the asset is overstated.

findings.headline: Audit opinion remains unresolved after three years in reset; qualified opinion is still uncertain.
findings.detail: The council has not obtained sufficient assurance over all closing balances and in-year movements despite two years of focused work. The auditors are still considering whether to issue a qualified opinion or a disclaimer for 2024/25. The lack of assurance over brought-forward balances from 2023/24 (which had a disclaimer) cascades through the current year's comparative figures.
findings.matters: An auditor unable to give clean assurance on the financial statements after extended recovery work signals fundamental reporting control weaknesses that lenders rely on to understand council finances.
findings.figures: Lack of assurance over Property, Plant & Equipment balances and Reserves balances; backstop date for completion is 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we have not yet obtained sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances.

news_drafts.headline: Worthing's treasury budget significantly underspent partly because project interest was capitalized to avoid revenue overspend on Integrated Care Centre
news_drafts.lead: Interest capitalization deferred revenue pressure; without it, the council would have faced a £300k overspend on treasury costs, indicating tight affordability margins on this major project

news_drafts.headline: Energy price shock threatens further inflation spike and rate increases: treasury advisors flag risk of CPI breaching 4.5% later in 2026
news_drafts.lead: If energy-driven inflation spike materializes, refinancing costs will be significantly higher than currently budgeted; lenders assess councils' resilience to sustained high rate environment

news_drafts.headline: Interest rate environment sharply reversed from expectation: Bank Rate held at 3.75% and treasury advisors now expect rises to 4-4.25%, not cuts
news_drafts.lead: Refinancing of maturing debt (23-25% of portfolio under 12 months) will occur at materially higher rates than forecast; both councils face higher financing costs and must refinance debt when rates are elevated
